screens.title: Inheritance and Polymorphism
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how inheritance and polymorphism help you model game entities that share core data and behavior while still letting each type act differently. We will build on the idea that a Player, an Enemy, and a Coin can all be 'game objects' with position and draw logic, yet each must implement its own unique actions. You will see how to organize shared members into a base class, control access with public and protected, and then use virtual functions to achieve dynamic dispatch so calls select the right behavior at runtime. We'll also contrast overriding a base method with overloading different signatures, and introduce abstract classes and pure virtual functions to force derived classes to implement required behavior. Along the way, we'll highlight practical pitfalls — like when destructors must be virtual and what object slicing means — and give concrete code examples you can adapt to your projects. By the end, you will be able to design a simple entity hierarchy, implement polymorphic loops that update and draw mixed entities, and reason about safety and ownership when deleting through base pointers.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Inheritance & Polymorphism
Inheritance and Polymorphism
Create diverse game entities that share core behavior while customizing actions
In this lesson
You will learn how to define a base GameObject, extend it with derived types, and use virtual functions to call the right method at runtime. You will also see when to use protected members, abstract classes, and virtual destructors.
Why this matters
When your game grows, inheritance reduces duplication and makes entity behavior extensible without rewriting core logic.
Explore key topics
Base class design
Pick shared data like position and default Update/Draw behaviors.
Virtual functions
Mark methods virtual to enable polymorphic override by derived types.
Abstract interfaces
Use pure virtuals to require methods such as Attack or TakeDamage.

Use this map as a design checklist: common state and virtual behavior live in the base; unique state and behavior belong in derived classes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will develop four concrete skills that map directly to building robust game object hierarchies. First, you will explain inheritance and why it models 'is-a' relationships, using examples such as a Goblin being an Enemy and an Enemy being a Character. This matters because clear hierarchies reduce duplicated code and make behaviour easier to reason about. Second, you will implement single inheritance in C++: declare base and derived classes, choose appropriate access specifiers, and call base constructors. You will practice using protected members to allow derived classes controlled access to shared state. Third, you will use polymorphism through virtual functions and base-class pointers and references. You will write loops that operate on a vector of base pointers and observe the right derived Update or Draw running at runtime. Finally, you will design abstract classes and pure virtual functions to define required interfaces, and you will understand why destructors should be virtual in polymorphic hierarchies. Each objective includes a short practice step so you can verify behavior in a small main loop.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice Focus
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on practical checks you can perform as you code. First, verify access control: make a protected member in the base class and access it from a derived class; confirm external code cannot access it. This validates encapsulation while allowing inheritance. Second, test polymorphic behavior by creating a vector of base pointers, push back a mix of Player, Enemy, and Collectable objects, then call Update and Draw in a loop to observe runtime selection of methods. Third, intentionally declare a pure virtual in a base class to confirm the compiler prevents instantiation of the base; then implement it in derived classes to make them concrete. Finally, practice safe cleanup: delete derived objects through base pointers and confirm destructors run in the correct order by using virtual destructors. Each check maps to a real bug you would otherwise encounter in a game loop, so these practice steps are high-leverage for debugging and design confidence.

screens.title: What is Inheritance?
screens.narratorSegment: Inheritance is a mechanism that lets you create a new class based on an existing one, allowing the new class to reuse and extend members from the base. In game development this models natural hierarchies: a Goblin is an Enemy, an Enemy is a Character, and a Character might be a GameObject with position and shared update logic. The practical benefit is reducing duplicated code — shared state such as position, name, and default draw logic belong in the base. When you derive a class, public and protected members are available to children; private members remain hidden to preserve encapsulation. A concrete example: put xPos and yPos and a virtual Draw in GameObject so Player and Enemy inherit position and can each implement Draw to add unique visuals. A common misconception is to put every shared function into the base even when behavior differs widely; instead, factor only truly shared responsibilities. Also avoid deep multiple inheritance for simple entity systems; prefer single inheritance with composition for extra capabilities. To check your design, ask whether derived classes will share the same data layout and whether the base owns behavior that makes sense as a default. If not, consider an abstract base or a component instead. What shared responsibilities would you extract from your current game objects?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Inheritance lets derived classes reuse and extend base class attributes and behavior, modeling 'is-a' relationships.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is Inheritance?
Core definition
A derived class is created from a base class and inherits its members. Use protected for controlled reuse.
Quick checklist
  • Extract truly shared state like position and name into the base.
  • Keep derived-specific state private to derived classes.
  • Use protected for members intended only for derived classes.
Example
GameObject: xPos, yPos, virtual Draw(). Player inherits position and overrides Draw to show health.
Key Takeaway

Extract shared state and behaviors into a base class, but avoid forcing unrelated behavior into the hierarchy.

Design analogy
Think of the base as a template for shared identity and minimal default behaviour. Derived classes add specialized traits.
Base: GameObject
xPos, yPos, name, virtual Update(), virtual Draw()
Derived: Player
health, score, overrides Update() and Draw()
Derived: Enemy
attackPower, AI in Update()
Derived: Collectable
value, simple Update() for sparkle
Misconception: Inheritance is not always the right tool. Use it when you need a true 'is-a' relation; prefer composition for loosely related behaviors.

screens.title: Access Control: public, protected, private
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding access control is essential when designing class hierarchies. Public members are part of the class's external interface and can be used by any code that has access to the object. Private members hide implementation details completely from derived classes and external code. Protected members sit between these extremes: they are hidden from outside code but visible to derived classes. In game entities, protected is frequently the right choice for shared internal state like position or animation state because derived classes need to manipulate those details, but external systems should not. Concrete example: declare xPos and yPos as protected in GameObject so Player and Enemy update positions directly while preventing arbitrary external writes. A typical misconception is to make everything public for convenience; this reduces encapsulation and increases coupling. Another trap is overusing protected for variables that should be accessed via protected getter/setter methods — direct protected fields can make maintenance harder. When you need strict external invariants, prefer private members with protected or public accessor functions. Finally, remember that access control does not affect object layout or polymorphism — it only controls compile-time visibility and should be chosen to express intent and keep modules decoupled.

keyIdea.title: Access control
keyIdea.text: Use protected for members that derived classes must access, private to hide internal details, and public for the external API.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Access Control
Access quick-reference
Public
Visible to all code.
Protected
Visible to derived classes only.
Private
Visible only inside the class.
Example decision: store positional state as protected so derived classes can implement movement without exposing internals to the rest of the engine.
Key Takeaway
Choose access to express intent: public for API, protected for inheritance, private for encapsulation.
Common mistakes
  • Making everything public because it's 'easier' — this breaks encapsulation.
  • Using protected fields as a shortcut for poor design instead of accessors.
  • Expecting access specifiers to enforce runtime safety — they only control compile-time visibility.
Mini example
// Base class snippet
class GameObject {
protected:
  float xPos, yPos; // derived classes can use these
public:
  void SetPosition(float x, float y) { xPos = x; yPos = y; }
};

// Player can read and write xPos directly in its methods

screens.title: Implementing Single Inheritance in C++
screens.narratorSegment: Let's step through a minimal, practical example of single inheritance in C++. The base GameObject holds shared state like name and position, declares virtual Update and Draw methods, and provides a virtual destructor to ensure proper cleanup. A Player class publicly inherits GameObject, calls the base constructor in its initializer list, and overrides Update and Draw using the override keyword. Concrete example: the GameObject constructor initializes name and position and prints creation messages; Player's constructor calls GameObject(name,x,y) and sets health. When you create a Player via new and store it in a GameObject pointer, calls to Update and Draw are polymorphic because the base declares these methods virtual. A common pitfall is forgetting the virtual destructor — deleting the Player through a GameObject pointer will not call Player's destructor unless the base destructor is virtual, potentially leaking resources. Another issue is accidentally creating an overloaded function rather than overriding due to signature mismatch; using override helps the compiler catch that. This walkthrough will help you write safe constructors, proper overrides, and predictable polymorphic behavior in your entity hierarchy. Implementing Single Inheritance in C++ means call the base constructor, use override for clarity, and always make the base destructor virtual when using polymorphism.. In practical terms, base and derived classes with constructors and overrides. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Implementing Inheritance
Key code excerpt
#include <iostream>
class GameObject {
protected:
  float xPos, yPos;
  std::string name;
public:
  GameObject(const std::string& objName, float x, float y)
    : name(objName), xPos(x), yPos(y) {}
  virtual ~GameObject() {}
  virtual void Update(float deltaTime) { std::cout << "base update" << std::endl; }
  virtual void Draw() const { std::cout << "base draw" << std::endl; }
};

class Player : public GameObject {
  int health;
public:
  Player(const std::string& n, float x, float y, int h)
    : GameObject(n,x,y), health(h) {}
  void Update(float deltaTime) override { /* player logic */ }
  void Draw() const override { /* player draw */ }
};
Explanations
  • Base constructor initializes shared state; derived calls it in the initializer list.
  • Declare virtual methods in the base to enable dynamic dispatch.
  • Use override so the compiler flags signature mismatches.
  • Make the base destructor virtual when using dynamic allocation with base pointers.
Example scenario
You create Player via new and push into std::vector<GameObject*>. Update and Draw will call Player's versions at runtime.
Misconception check: calling a base method from a derived override is optional. Use GameObject::Update(deltaTime) inside overrides if you want default behavior combined with specialized logic.

screens.title: Polymorphism and Virtual Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Polymorphism allows code that works with a base type to correctly invoke derived behavior at runtime. The mechanism in C++ is virtual functions. When a member is declared virtual in the base class, calls through base pointers or references use dynamic dispatch to locate the implementation corresponding to the object's actual type. A typical pattern in games is a vector of base pointers: std::vector<GameObject*> holds Players, Enemies, and Collectables; calling Update on each pointer runs the correct derived Update. A concrete example is having GameObject::Update declared virtual and overridden in Player and Enemy; during the game loop, you don't need to know which derived type each pointer refers to. A misconception is thinking virtual adds runtime overhead that's always unacceptable — while it does introduce indirection, the clarity and extensibility often outweigh the cost in high-level game logic. Another pitfall is accidentally defining non-virtual functions in the base and expecting overriding; that won't dispatch polymorphically. To verify correctness, compile with the override keyword in derived methods and run a small loop that prints which Update executes. The core takeaway: virtual functions let you write unified loops over heterogeneous objects safely and expressively.

keyIdea.title: Polymorphism
keyIdea.text: Virtual functions enable the runtime to call the appropriate derived method through base pointers or references.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Polymorphism
Polymorphic loop example
std::vector<GameObject*> gameEntities;
gameEntities.push_back(new Player("Hero",0,0,100));
gameEntities.push_back(new Enemy("Goblin",5,5,10));

for (GameObject* e : gameEntities) {
  e->Update(deltaTime); // calls derived Update
  e->Draw();             // calls derived Draw
}
This loop demonstrates that the same call can produce different behavior depending on each object's actual type.
Checks and pitfalls
  • Ensure the base declares methods as virtual for polymorphism to work.
  • Use override in derived classes to catch signature errors at compile time.
  • Remember the virtual destructor to allow proper cleanup.
Key Takeaway
Virtual functions let you write general algorithms that operate on different concrete types without branchy type checks.

screens.title: Overriding vs Overloading
screens.narratorSegment: Function overriding and function overloading are different concepts that are sometimes confused. Overriding happens when a derived class provides a new implementation for a virtual function declared in the base class using the same signature. This supports polymorphism: the call resolves to the derived implementation at runtime. Overloading, by contrast, defines multiple functions with the same name but different parameter lists within the same scope or class. Overloading is a compile-time resolution based on argument types and counts. Concrete example: if GameObject declares virtual void Update(float), and Player implements void Update(float) override, that's overriding. If Player declares void Update(float) and void Update(int), those are overloads — the compiler picks which to call from the call site. A common trap is accidentally creating an overload in the derived class because of a slightly different signature, which prevents overriding and breaks polymorphism. The override keyword is an easy safeguard: if the signature does not match a virtual base, the compiler issues an error. When designing APIs, keep virtual interfaces stable to avoid accidental overloads and prefer clear signatures that capture the intended polymorphic behavior.

keyIdea.title: Distinction
keyIdea.text: Overriding replaces base behavior at runtime; overloading provides multiple compile-time variants in the same scope.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Overriding vs Overloading
Side-by-side
Overriding
Derived provides same signature implementation; virtual dispatch runs derived at runtime.
Overloading
Multiple functions share a name but differ by parameter lists; resolved at compile time.
Use override to ensure you are overriding. If you accidentally change a parameter type in the derived method, you'll create an overload instead, and calls through base pointers will not dispatch to your intended function.
Mini example
// Overriding
virtual void Update(float dt);
void Update(float dt) override; // derived override works polymorphically

// Overloading
void Update(int steps); // overload, not polymorphic
Misconception: Same name implies overriding — always verify signatures match exactly when polymorphism is intended.

screens.title: Abstract Classes and Pure Virtual Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Abstract classes and pure virtual functions allow you to require that derived classes implement certain behaviors. A pure virtual function is declared by assigning = 0 in the base declaration, for example virtual void Attack() = 0;. Any class with at least one pure virtual is abstract and cannot be instantiated. This is useful in game systems where the base has no sensible default implementation for an action — for instance, Character may declare virtual void Attack() = 0 to force Player, Enemy, and NPC to implement Attack in their own way. An abstract base functions as a contract: it documents and enforces what derived classes must provide. A concrete example: create a Damageable abstract class with virtual void TakeDamage(int) = 0; then every entity that can take damage implements that method. A common error is forgetting to implement all pure virtuals in a derived class, which itself remains abstract; the compiler will tell you which functions are missing. Another design note: abstract classes can still provide utility non-pure methods or protected helpers to share common code while leaving the core behavior abstract. Use abstract classes to express required capabilities clearly and let the compiler help enforce correct implementations.

keyIdea.title: Abstract class
keyIdea.text: Use pure virtuals to declare required methods that derived classes must implement, turning the base into an interface-like contract.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Abstract Classes
Why use pure virtuals?
They force derived classes to implement essential behavior and prevent incorrect instantiation of incomplete types.
Example interface
class Damageable {
public:
  virtual ~Damageable() {}
  virtual void TakeDamage(int amount) = 0; // pure virtual
};

class Enemy : public Damageable {
  void TakeDamage(int amount) override { /* reduce health */ }
};
Design notes
  • An abstract base can still offer helper methods or protected utilities.
  • Use pure virtuals when the base has no meaningful default behavior.
  • The compiler tells you which pure virtuals remain unimplemented.
Key Takeaway

Treat abstract classes as contracts that document required behaviors and enable safe polymorphic design.

screens.title: Virtual Destructors and Safe Cleanup
screens.narratorSegment: When working with polymorphism and dynamic allocation, correct cleanup is critical. If you allocate derived objects with new and store them in base-class pointers, deleting those pointers must invoke both the derived and base destructors. In C++ this only happens when the base destructor is virtual. If it is not, deleting a derived object through a base pointer calls only the base destructor, leaving derived-specific cleanup unexecuted and potentially causing resource leaks. A concrete example: if Player allocates memory or owns file handles cleaned by Player's destructor, deleting via GameObject* ptr = new Player(...) without virtual ~GameObject() will skip Player's cleanup. The fix is simple: declare virtual ~GameObject() in the base. Also pair each new with delete, or better, use smart pointers to automate lifetime. A common misconception is believing destructors are always called in reverse construction order; that is true only when the destructor chain runs. Making the base destructor virtual guarantees the entire chain executes. As a safety habit, mark base destructors virtual in any class designed for polymorphic use. Consider static analysis and code reviews to ensure ownership patterns are clear and destructors are properly declared.

A common misconception is believing destructors are always called in reverse construction order; that is true only when the destructor chain runs. Making the base destructor virtual guarantees the entire chain executes. As a safety habit, mark base destructors virtual in any class designed for polymorphic use. Consider static analysis and code reviews to ensure ownership patterns are clear and destructors are properly declared.

keyIdea.title: Destructor rule
keyIdea.text: If a class is used polymorphically, give its destructor virtual to ensure derived destructors run on deletion.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Virtual Destructors
Why it matters
Deleting a derived object via a base pointer without a virtual base destructor skips derived cleanup and can leak resources.
Code example
class GameObject {
public:
  virtual ~GameObject() { std::cout << "Base destructor" << std::endl; }
};

class Player : public GameObject {
public:
  ~Player() { /* free player resources */ }
};

GameObject* p = new Player();
delete p; // calls Player::~Player() then GameObject::~GameObject()
Practical guidance
  • Always make destructors virtual in polymorphic base classes.
  • Prefer smart pointers to manage ownership and avoid manual delete.
  • Use RAII for resource management inside derived classes.
Key Takeaway
Virtual destructors ensure full destructor chains run and prevent subtle resource leaks when using polymorphism.

screens.title: Extending the Hierarchy: Collectable, Coin, Potion
screens.narratorSegment: This screen walks through the activity that extends GameObject with a Collectable base and coin and potion derived classes. The Collectable class inherits from GameObject and adds a private value member with a constructor initializing it. It overrides Update and Draw to show collectable-specific behavior and provides a GetValue method. Coin and Potion then derive from Collectable: they call Collectable's constructor and override Update with unique messages like 'rotating' or 'bubbling.' In practice, you will add Coin and Potion instances to the same std::vector<GameObject*> used for Player and Enemy. During the game loop, calling Update and Draw on each pointer runs the correct collectable behavior. This demonstrates how inheritance and polymorphism scale as you add new categories of objects without changing the main loop. A common mistake is forgetting to initialize the collectable's value in derived constructors — always forward constructor arguments into the base initializer list. Also ensure any resources owned by collectables are properly cleaned up in destructors and, if needed, guard access to value with a constant getter. Try adding Coin and Potion and observe the polymorphic updates in your loop.

keyIdea.text: Add a specialized base (Collectable) to group related types, then derive concrete classes like Coin and Potion that override behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Collectable Example
Collectable hierarchy (excerpt)
class Collectable : public GameObject {
private:
  int value;
public:
  Collectable(const std::string& name, float x, float y, int v)
    : GameObject(name,x,y), value(v) {}
  void Update(float dt) override { std::cout << name << " is sparkling." << std::endl; }
  void Draw() const override { std::cout << "Drawing " << name << " (Value: " << value << ")" << std::endl; }
  int GetValue() const { return value; }
};

class Coin : public Collectable {
public:
  Coin(float x, float y, int v) : Collectable("Coin", x, y, v) {}
  void Update(float dt) override { std::cout << name << " is rotating." << std::endl; }
};
Practical notes
  • Forward constructor parameters to base classes using initializer lists.
  • Override Update to give each collectable its animation or behavior.
  • Keep value private and expose a const getter for safe read access.
Key Takeaway
Use intermediate base classes like Collectable to group related behaviour and then create small, focused concrete classes for specific items.

screens.title: Slicing, Ownership, and Practical Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: As you apply inheritance and polymorphism, be aware of common pitfalls that lead to bugs. Object slicing occurs when you assign a derived object to a base object by value, e. g., GameObject base = player;. This copies only the base portion and discards derived-specific data, breaking polymorphism and losing state. The safe pattern is to use pointers or references for polymorphic behavior. Ownership and lifetime also cause problems: if you allocate derived objects with new and store raw pointers in a vector, forgetting to delete them will leak memory; deleting without a virtual destructor will skip derived cleanup. Prefer smart pointers like std::unique_ptr or std::shared_ptr to clarify ownership and ensure automatic destruction. Another practical issue is accidentally changing a method signature in a derived class, which creates an overload instead of override; the override keyword mitigates this. Performance concerns sometimes make developers avoid virtual functions, but design clarity and future extensibility often win for entity-level logic. The takeaway is to pick safe patterns: use references/pointers for polymorphism, smart pointers for ownership, and override/virtual keywords to make intentions explicit. Slicing, Ownership, and Practical Pitfalls means avoid slicing by using pointers/references, prefer smart pointers for ownership, and use override/virtual to prevent signature errors.. In practical terms, avoid runtime surprises when using inheritance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Avoid slicing by using pointers/references, prefer smart pointers for ownership, and use override/virtual to prevent signature errors.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Slicing & Ownership
Object slicing example
Player p("Hero",0,0,100);
GameObject g = p; // slicing: g contains only GameObject part

// Use pointer instead:
GameObject* gp = &p; // polymorphic calls will work
Slicing silently removes derived data. Always prefer pointers or references when you intend polymorphism.
Ownership guidance
  • Use std::unique_ptr<GameObject> in containers to express ownership and avoid manual delete.
  • When sharing ownership, use std::shared_ptr carefully to avoid cycles.
  • Always document ownership rules for collections of base pointers.
Warning
Using raw new/delete together with non-virtual destructors is a common source of memory leaks; favor RAII and smart pointers.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential ideas you should take away. First, inheritance models 'is-a' relationships and helps you factor shared state and behavior into a common base. Second, virtual functions enable polymorphism so calls through base pointers select derived implementations at runtime. Third, abstract classes and pure virtual functions act as contracts that force derived classes to implement essential behavior. These three items form the backbone of safely extending entity systems. When designing your systems, remember to use protected members only when derived classes need direct access, keep external APIs public and stable, and prefer composition when inheritance does not express a true 'is-a' relationship. Also remember the practical rules: use override to avoid accidental overloads, declare base destructors virtual for safe cleanup, and avoid slicing by using pointers or references. These concepts together let you build scalable, maintainable game object hierarchies.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how inheritance and polymorphism help you model game entities that share core data and behavior while still letting each type act differently. We will build on the idea that a Player, an Enemy, and a Coin can all be 'game objects' with position and draw logic, yet each must implement its own unique actions. You will see how to organize shared members into a base class, control access with public and protected, and then use virtual functions to achieve dynamic dispatch so calls select the right behavior at runtime. We'll also contrast overriding a base method with overloading different signatures, and introduce abstract classes and pure virtual functions to force derived classes to implement required behavior. Along the way, we'll highlight practical pitfalls — like when destructors must be virtual and what object slicing means — and give concrete code examples you can adapt to your projects. By the end, you will be able to design a simple entity hierarchy, implement polymorphic loops that update and draw mixed entities, and reason about safety and ownership when deleting through base pointers.

In this chapter you will develop four concrete skills that map directly to building robust game object hierarchies. First, you will explain inheritance and why it models 'is-a' relationships, using examples such as a Goblin being an Enemy and an Enemy being a Character. This matters because clear hierarchies reduce duplicated code and make behaviour easier to reason about. Second, you will implement single inheritance in C++: declare base and derived classes, choose appropriate access specifiers, and call base constructors. You will practice using protected members to allow derived classes controlled access to shared state. Third, you will use polymorphism through virtual functions and base-class pointers and references. You will write loops that operate on a vector of base pointers and observe the right derived Update or Draw running at runtime. Finally, you will design abstract classes and pure virtual functions to define required interfaces, and you will understand why destructors should be virtual in polymorphic hierarchies. Each objective includes a short practice step so you can verify behavior in a small main loop.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical checks you can perform as you code. First, verify access control: make a protected member in the base class and access it from a derived class; confirm external code cannot access it. This validates encapsulation while allowing inheritance. Second, test polymorphic behavior by creating a vector of base pointers, push back a mix of Player, Enemy, and Collectable objects, then call Update and Draw in a loop to observe runtime selection of methods. Third, intentionally declare a pure virtual in a base class to confirm the compiler prevents instantiation of the base; then implement it in derived classes to make them concrete. Finally, practice safe cleanup: delete derived objects through base pointers and confirm destructors run in the correct order by using virtual destructors. Each check maps to a real bug you would otherwise encounter in a game loop, so these practice steps are high-leverage for debugging and design confidence.

Inheritance is a mechanism that lets you create a new class based on an existing one, allowing the new class to reuse and extend members from the base. In game development this models natural hierarchies: a Goblin is an Enemy, an Enemy is a Character, and a Character might be a GameObject with position and shared update logic. The practical benefit is reducing duplicated code — shared state such as position, name, and default draw logic belong in the base. When you derive a class, public and protected members are available to children; private members remain hidden to preserve encapsulation. A concrete example: put xPos and yPos and a virtual Draw in GameObject so Player and Enemy inherit position and can each implement Draw to add unique visuals. A common misconception is to put every shared function into the base even when behavior differs widely; instead, factor only truly shared responsibilities. Also avoid deep multiple inheritance for simple entity systems; prefer single inheritance with composition for extra capabilities. To check your design, ask whether derived classes will share the same data layout and whether the base owns behavior that makes sense as a default. If not, consider an abstract base or a component instead. What shared responsibilities would you extract from your current game objects?

Understanding access control is essential when designing class hierarchies. Public members are part of the class's external interface and can be used by any code that has access to the object. Private members hide implementation details completely from derived classes and external code. Protected members sit between these extremes: they are hidden from outside code but visible to derived classes. In game entities, protected is frequently the right choice for shared internal state like position or animation state because derived classes need to manipulate those details, but external systems should not. Concrete example: declare xPos and yPos as protected in GameObject so Player and Enemy update positions directly while preventing arbitrary external writes. A typical misconception is to make everything public for convenience; this reduces encapsulation and increases coupling. Another trap is overusing protected for variables that should be accessed via protected getter/setter methods — direct protected fields can make maintenance harder. When you need strict external invariants, prefer private members with protected or public accessor functions. Finally, remember that access control does not affect object layout or polymorphism — it only controls compile-time visibility and should be chosen to express intent and keep modules decoupled.

Let's step through a minimal, practical example of single inheritance in C++. The base GameObject holds shared state like name and position, declares virtual Update and Draw methods, and provides a virtual destructor to ensure proper cleanup. A Player class publicly inherits GameObject, calls the base constructor in its initializer list, and overrides Update and Draw using the override keyword. Concrete example: the GameObject constructor initializes name and position and prints creation messages; Player's constructor calls GameObject(name,x,y) and sets health. When you create a Player via new and store it in a GameObject pointer, calls to Update and Draw are polymorphic because the base declares these methods virtual. A common pitfall is forgetting the virtual destructor — deleting the Player through a GameObject pointer will not call Player's destructor unless the base destructor is virtual, potentially leaking resources. Another issue is accidentally creating an overloaded function rather than overriding due to signature mismatch; using override helps the compiler catch that. This walkthrough will help you write safe constructors, proper overrides, and predictable polymorphic behavior in your entity hierarchy. Implementing Single Inheritance in C++ means call the base constructor, use override for clarity, and always make the base destructor virtual when using polymorphism.. In practical terms, base and derived classes with constructors and overrides. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Polymorphism allows code that works with a base type to correctly invoke derived behavior at runtime. The mechanism in C++ is virtual functions. When a member is declared virtual in the base class, calls through base pointers or references use dynamic dispatch to locate the implementation corresponding to the object's actual type. A typical pattern in games is a vector of base pointers: std::vector<GameObject*> holds Players, Enemies, and Collectables; calling Update on each pointer runs the correct derived Update. A concrete example is having GameObject::Update declared virtual and overridden in Player and Enemy; during the game loop, you don't need to know which derived type each pointer refers to. A misconception is thinking virtual adds runtime overhead that's always unacceptable — while it does introduce indirection, the clarity and extensibility often outweigh the cost in high-level game logic. Another pitfall is accidentally defining non-virtual functions in the base and expecting overriding; that won't dispatch polymorphically. To verify correctness, compile with the override keyword in derived methods and run a small loop that prints which Update executes. The core takeaway: virtual functions let you write unified loops over heterogeneous objects safely and expressively.

Function overriding and function overloading are different concepts that are sometimes confused. Overriding happens when a derived class provides a new implementation for a virtual function declared in the base class using the same signature. This supports polymorphism: the call resolves to the derived implementation at runtime. Overloading, by contrast, defines multiple functions with the same name but different parameter lists within the same scope or class. Overloading is a compile-time resolution based on argument types and counts. Concrete example: if GameObject declares virtual void Update(float), and Player implements void Update(float) override, that's overriding. If Player declares void Update(float) and void Update(int), those are overloads — the compiler picks which to call from the call site. A common trap is accidentally creating an overload in the derived class because of a slightly different signature, which prevents overriding and breaks polymorphism. The override keyword is an easy safeguard: if the signature does not match a virtual base, the compiler issues an error. When designing APIs, keep virtual interfaces stable to avoid accidental overloads and prefer clear signatures that capture the intended polymorphic behavior.

Abstract classes and pure virtual functions allow you to require that derived classes implement certain behaviors. A pure virtual function is declared by assigning = 0 in the base declaration, for example virtual void Attack() = 0;. Any class with at least one pure virtual is abstract and cannot be instantiated. This is useful in game systems where the base has no sensible default implementation for an action — for instance, Character may declare virtual void Attack() = 0 to force Player, Enemy, and NPC to implement Attack in their own way. An abstract base functions as a contract: it documents and enforces what derived classes must provide. A concrete example: create a Damageable abstract class with virtual void TakeDamage(int) = 0; then every entity that can take damage implements that method. A common error is forgetting to implement all pure virtuals in a derived class, which itself remains abstract; the compiler will tell you which functions are missing. Another design note: abstract classes can still provide utility non-pure methods or protected helpers to share common code while leaving the core behavior abstract. Use abstract classes to express required capabilities clearly and let the compiler help enforce correct implementations.

When working with polymorphism and dynamic allocation, correct cleanup is critical. If you allocate derived objects with new and store them in base-class pointers, deleting those pointers must invoke both the derived and base destructors. In C++ this only happens when the base destructor is virtual. If it is not, deleting a derived object through a base pointer calls only the base destructor, leaving derived-specific cleanup unexecuted and potentially causing resource leaks. A concrete example: if Player allocates memory or owns file handles cleaned by Player's destructor, deleting via GameObject* ptr = new Player(...) without virtual ~GameObject() will skip Player's cleanup. The fix is simple: declare virtual ~GameObject() in the base. Also pair each new with delete, or better, use smart pointers to automate lifetime. A common misconception is believing destructors are always called in reverse construction order; that is true only when the destructor chain runs. Making the base destructor virtual guarantees the entire chain executes. As a safety habit, mark base destructors virtual in any class designed for polymorphic use. Consider static analysis and code reviews to ensure ownership patterns are clear and destructors are properly declared.
